questions.q: When an iteration's submission fails due to a circuit validation error, what does this project's error-handling logic do, per the Lesson 12 decision table it applies?
options: Logs it as a code bug and does NOT retry, since retrying an invalid circuit would fail identically every time
Immediately falls back to a classical simulator without checking the failure reason
Retries up to 3 times with exponential backoff, the same as a device-offline failure
Ignores the failure and proceeds to the next iteration as if it succeeded
questions.explain: Per the Lesson 12 decision table, a validation failure is a classical code bug that will fail identically on retry -- the correct response is to log it and not retry, unlike a device-offline or queue-timeout failure.

questions.q: In the running cost ledger, if iteration 23 fails once (billed $12.00) before succeeding on retry (billed another $12.00), how should this be recorded?
options: As two separate $12.00 ledger entries (one FAILED, one DONE), making the wasted spend from the failed attempt visible rather than silently merged into a single entry
As a single $12.00 entry, since only the successful attempt should be logged
As a single $24.00 entry with no indication that a failure occurred
As a $0.00 entry, since failed attempts are never billed
questions.explain: Logging both attempts separately (one FAILED at $12.00, one DONE at $12.00) makes the $12.00 of wasted spend from the failure visible in the ledger, consistent with the orchestration lab's requirement to surface wasted-retry cost as its own line item.

questions.q: The cost circuit-breaker is set to $1,200 (25% headroom above the $960 planned budget). What does the circuit-breaker do, and when is it checked?
options: It checks cumulative ledger cost after every submission, independent of the iteration counter, and halts the loop with an alert if cumulative cost crosses $1,200
It only checks cost once, after all 80 iterations complete
It checks only the iteration counter, ignoring actual dollar cost
It automatically increases the budget ceiling whenever cost approaches it
questions.explain: The circuit-breaker is checked after every submission (not just at the end or based on iteration count alone) and halts the loop immediately if cumulative spend crosses the $1,200 ceiling, exactly as the Lesson 5 Mistake 3 fix specifies.

questions.q: Why does the project use fault injection (forcing a specific submission to return FAILED on command) instead of waiting for a real device failure to test error handling?
options: Real device failures are too rare and unpredictable to reliably trigger during testing, while fault injection lets specific failure scenarios (device-offline, validation failure, repeated failures) be tested deterministically
Fault injection is required by all cloud quantum providers before deployment
Real failures cannot be simulated in any software system
Fault injection eliminates the need for a cost ledger
questions.explain: Deterministic fault injection lets the test harness verify specific error-handling paths (backoff-and-retry, no-retry-on-validation-failure, fallback-after-exhausted-retries) on command, rather than depending on an unpredictable real failure occurring at a convenient testing moment.

questions.q: What should a completed or halted run's log allow a reviewer to determine WITHOUT re-running the system?
options: Total cost, total wall-clock time, which iterations failed/retried and their cost, whether any fallback was used, and the final converged value with its standard error
Only whether the run succeeded or failed, with no further detail
Only the source code of the orchestration layer
Nothing; logs are not expected to answer any of these questions
questions.explain: This is the same post-hoc answerability requirement from the orchestration lab (Lesson 14), now applied concretely: the log must let a reviewer reconstruct cost, timing, failures, and the final statistically-reported result without re-executing anything.
